summary: Specifies deriving the content-encryption or content-authenticated-encryption key in CMS using HKDF with SHA-256. Doing so protects against an attacker who manipulates the content-encryption (or content-authenticated-encryption) algorithm identifier.

eli5.summary: Instead of using a secret key directly, you mix it up to make a fresh working key. That stops sneaky swaps of the settings.

questions: how to derive cms encryption keys
how does cms stop algorithm identifier tampering
how does cms derive the content encryption key
subtitle: Mixing the algorithm identifier into the CMS encryption key so an attacker cannot swap the cipher and read the message.

tldr.problem: An attacker who can change the algorithm identifier on an encrypted CMS message can turn an authenticated-encryption message into a fake AES-CBC one and trick the recipient into revealing decrypted blocks.
tldr.mechanism: The sender derives a new key with HKDF and SHA-256 from the original key and the DER-encoded AlgorithmIdentifier, so any change to that identifier makes the recipient derive a different key.
tldr.outcome: A tampered algorithm identifier now produces a useless key instead of leaking plaintext. The cost is one extra algorithm identifier, id-alg-cek-hkdf-sha256, that signals the mitigation.

today: RFC 9709 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2025, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The IANA registrations in the text show the identifier has been assigned.

sections.title: The Attack and the Mitigation
sections.content:
The Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) carries encrypted content in three content types: enveloped-data and encrypted-data (RFC 5652) and authenticated-enveloped-data (RFC 5083). Each names its encryption algorithm in an algorithm identifier that is not itself protected by the content key.

The RFC describes an attack presented at IETF 118. The attacker intercepts a message that uses AES-CCM or AES-GCM, rewrites it as a "garbage" enveloped-data message made of AES-CBC guess blocks, and sends it to the victim. If the victim reveals the decryption result, any block that matches the attacker's guess exposes that plaintext block. With highly structured messages, one block can be the only sensitive part.

The fix is to make the encryption key depend on the unmodified algorithm identifier. The mitigation has three parts: recipients advertise support in S/MIME Capabilities, senders carry the id-alg-cek-hkdf-sha256 identifier as the contentEncryptionAlgorithm as a flag, and encryption uses a derived key, CEK' = HKDF(CEK, AlgorithmIdentifier).
sections.eli5: A trickster could swap the instructions on a locked message so it gets opened a different way. The fix ties the key to the instructions, so swapping them breaks the key.

sections.title: The CMS_CEK_HKDF_SHA256 Function
sections.content:
The derivation uses the HMAC-based Extract-and-Expand Key Derivation Function (HKDF, RFC 5869) with the SHA-256 hash. The input keying material (IKM) is the original key. The optional info input is the DER-encoded AlgorithmIdentifier, including its SEQUENCE tag (0x30), length and value. The output keying material (OKM) is the same size as the IKM.

The function first checks that the IKM length in octets is no more than 8160, and raises an error otherwise. It then uses the fixed salt The Cryptographic Message Syntax to run HKDF-Extract and produce a pseudorandom key (PRK), and HKDF-Expand over that PRK with the info and the original key length.

If an attacker changes the originator-provided AlgorithmIdentifier, the recipient derives a different key. The RFC deliberately allows only HKDF and only SHA-256. A new object identifier could be assigned later for another function, but keeping the design very simple is the stated priority.
sections.eli5: The key goes into a blender along with the instructions note and a fixed secret word. Change one ingredient and a completely different key comes out.

sections.title: The Algorithm Identifier and S/MIME Capabilities
sections.content:
The id-alg-cek-hkdf-sha256 object identifier is { iso(1) member-body(2) us(840) rsadsi(113549) pkcs(1) pkcs-9(9) id-smime(16) alg(3) 31 }. Its parameters field is required and has the ASN.1 type AlgorithmIdentifier. That parameter names the real content-encryption or content-authenticated-encryption algorithm and its own parameters.

An S/MIME client announces what it supports in the SMIMECapabilities attribute (RFC 8551). A client that supports this mechanism SHOULD include the identifier in that set, and the parameter MUST be absent. The encoding in hexadecimal is 30 0d 06 0b 2a 86 48 86 f7 0d 01 09 10 03 1f.

The ASN.1 definitions follow the conventions of RFC 5911, and the full module is in Appendix A.
sections.eli5: The new label on the box says "my real lock type is written inside the label." People can also say ahead of time that they understand this new kind of label.

sections.title: Using It with the Three CMS Content Types
sections.content:
The originator does the same three things for each content type. It puts id-alg-cek-hkdf-sha256 in contentEncryptionAlgorithm.algorithm of the EncryptedContentInfo structure. It sets the parameters field to the AlgorithmIdentifier of the cipher that will really be used. It then derives CEK' = CMS_CEK_HKDF_SHA256(CEK, ContentEncryptionAlgorithmIdentifier) and encrypts with CEK'.

For enveloped-data this expands step 4 of the construction in RFC 5652. For encrypted-data, where the key is managed by other means, the same steps apply. For authenticated-enveloped-data it expands step 5 of RFC 5083, so the attributes are authenticated and the content is authenticated and encrypted with CEK'.

The recipient sees the identifier in the algorithm field and derives CEK' before decrypting. If the identifier is absent, the recipient uses the original key CEK.
sections.eli5: Whoever packs the message mixes the key with the instructions first and locks with that mixed key. Whoever opens it does the same mixing before trying to open.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC picks one KDF to avoid negotiation. If a weakness is later found in it, a new attribute will have to be assigned for an alternative.

If the attacker removes the identifier, the recipient will not derive CEK', so the recipient is denied the content but the attacker learns nothing. If the attacker changes the parameters, the recipient derives a different CEK', which again does not help recover plaintext. The object identifier alone would be enough against the attack described, but including the parameters guards against a yet-to-be-discovered attack that manipulates only the parameters.

Implementations MUST protect the CEK and CEK', and MUST randomly generate content-encryption keys, since a weak pseudorandom number generator can leave little or no security. RFC 4086 gives guidance.

The privacy section adds that the message-digest attribute exposes an unencrypted hash of the plaintext, so the authenticated attributes SHOULD NOT contain it.
sections.eli5: If a trickster erases or changes the note, the receiver either cannot open the box or opens it with a wrong key, and the trickster still learns nothing.

sections.title: Operational and IANA Notes
sections.content:
CMS often protects messages in settings with spam and phishing. Recipients who accept unsolicited encrypted messages become more exposed because many defenses need the plaintext. The RFC suggests software provide other ways to handle unwanted traffic, such as rejecting or discarding encrypted messages unless they appear to come from a previously approved originator list.

IANA assigned decimal 80, id-mod-CMS-CEK-HKDF-SHA256-2023, in the SMI Security for S/MIME Module Identifier registry, and decimal 31, id-alg-cek-hkdf-sha256, in the SMI Security for S/MIME Algorithms registry.
sections.eli5: Because nobody can peek inside sealed boxes, it helps to accept boxes only from people on your approved list.

sections.title: Test Vectors
sections.content:
Appendix B gives two checks for the function, both with the same 16-byte input key c702e7d0a9e064b09ba55245fb733cf3. One uses an AES-128-GCM identifier with a 12-byte nonce and yields 2124ffb29fac4e0fbbc7d5d87492bff3. The other uses an AES-128-CBC identifier with a 16-byte IV and yields 9cd102c52f1e19ece8729b35bfeceb50.

The same key produces different outputs because the DER-encoded identifier differs, which shows the binding between the key and the algorithm description.
sections.eli5: The same starting key gives two different results because the two instruction notes differ.

viz.caption: THE DERIVATION AS GIVEN IN SECTION 2

data.title: CMS_CEK_HKDF_SHA256
data.code:
OKM_SIZE = len(IKM)  /* length in octets */
IF OKM_SIZE > 8160 THEN raise error

salt = "The Cryptographic Message Syntax"
PRK = HKDF-Extract(salt, IKM)

OKM = HKDF-Expand(PRK, info, OKM_SIZE)

viz.caption: THE THREE PARTS OF THE MITIGATION

items.title: Advertise
items.text: Recipients list id-alg-cek-hkdf-sha256, with no parameters, in S/MIME Capabilities.

items.title: Flag
items.text: Senders carry the identifier as contentEncryptionAlgorithm, with the real cipher in its parameters.
